terms.gloss: that’s not fair, you’re not playing fair
evidence: Ter. Haut. 91: ah nōn aequom facis
terms.comment: What people in comedy say to someone who is not dealing fairly with them; Plautus and Terence write the old spelling aequom. We have found no set phrase in the authors for cheating at a game, so the protest that it is unfair comes first. Of tripping a rival in a race, Cicero uses supplantāre (see the examples); of cheating someone out of something, see “cheat”; of copying in school, see “don’t cheat!”.
A plain sentence of ours with fallō, which Lewis & Short glosses “to deceive, trick, dupe, cheat”.

phrases.english: That’s cheating; you opened your eyes!

phrases.latin: at puerī lūdentēs: «rēx eris» ajunt, «sī rēctē faciēs»
phrases.english: but boys at play say, “You’ll be king if you play fair”

phrases.latin: quī stadium, inquit, currit, ēnītī et contendere dēbet quam maximē possit, ut vincat, supplantāre eum, quīcum certet, aut manū dēpellere nūllō modō dēbet
phrases.english: a man who runs a race, he says, ought to strain and strive as hard as he can to win, but he ought by no means to trip the man he is racing or push him away with his hand
